name: Asrikam
title: Asrikam – palace official, Davidic descendant, and other name bearers in the Old Testament
summary: Asrikam is a name borne by at least four different individuals in the Old Testament, spread across several centuries. The most historically prominent was the palace official (Hebrew nagid habbayit) who served under King Ahaz of Judah. He was killed by the Ephraimite Zichri during the Syro-Ephraimitic War around 735 BC, along with the king's son Maaseiah and the royal administrator Elkanah—an event that illustrates the war's dramatic consequences for the Judean court. In David's genealogy in 1 Chronicles, another Asrikam is mentioned as a son of Neariah and a descendant of King David through Zerubbabel's line, placing him in the post-exilic period and linking him to the royal Davidic lineage. A third Asrikam is recorded as a son of Azel among Saul's descendants in the tribe of Benjamin. Finally, a fourth Asrikam is mentioned in a Levitical context as an ancestor of Hashub, one of the Levites who settled in Jerusalem and resumed temple service after returning from the Babylonian exile.

keyEvents.title: Asrikam as the son of Azel
keyEvents.description: In the genealogy of Saul's descendants in the tribe of Benjamin, Asrikam is mentioned as one of the sons of Azel. The list is repeated in 1 Chron 9:44 in connection with the population of Jerusalem.

keyEvents.title: Asrikam killed as palace official during the Syro-Ephraimite War
keyEvents.description: During the Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 735 BC), Asrikam, the palace official of King Ahaz of Judah, was killed by the Ephraimite warrior Zikri. He was slain along with the king's son Maaseiah and the royal administrator Elkanah, marking a humiliating defeat for Judah.

keyEvents.title: Asrikam in David's lineage through Zerubbabel
keyEvents.description: Asrikam is mentioned as the son of Neariah and a descendant of King David through Zerubbabel in the Davidic genealogy. He is the brother of Eljoenai and Hizkia.

keyEvents.title: Asrikam among the Levites after the exile
keyEvents.description: An Asrikam is mentioned as an ancestor of the Levitical servant Hasshub in the lists of those who settled in Jerusalem after returning from Babylon. He appears in parallel genealogical lists in Chronicles and Nehemiah.

versions.summary: Asrikam is a person mentioned in several contexts in the Old Testament. He appears in the genealogies in 1 Chronicles as a descendant of David through Zerubbabel's line, and also as a Benjamite. Another Asrikam is mentioned as an official in King Ahaz's court who was killed by the Ephraimite Zikri during the war between Israel and Judah.
versions.title: Descendant of King David
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Descendant of King David' is misleading because there are several people named Asrikam in the Bible, and the profile covers all of them. Only one of them is a descendant of David. A more neutral title should reflect this.; [major] The profile covers multiple individuals named Asrikam from different time periods. Asrikam in Zerubbabel's line lived after the exile (the return period), not during the divided kingdom period. The official under King Ahaz belongs to the divided-kingdom era, while the Benjaminite in 1 Chron 9 and Neh 11 belongs to the return period. Since the profile combines several people, the era should reflect either the most prominent or the earliest one. 'divided-kingdom' can be defended for the official, but it is incorrect for the descendant of David.; [major] The lifespan 'around the 700s BC' fits only the official under King Ahaz. Asrikam in Zerubbabel's line lived around the 500s BC. Since the profile covers multiple people, the lifespan should reflect this range or be more general.; [minor] The summary is acceptable, but it lacks mention of Asrikam as son of Azel (1 Chron 8:38) and Asrikam in Nehemiah 11:15. The summary should cover all the different individuals mentioned.; [major] 'Leader' is too vague and only partially accurate. The official under Ahaz was a palace commander. Other Asrikams were not necessarily leaders. The roles should include 'palace commander' or 'official', and possibly 'Davidic descendant'.; [major] For the most prominent Asrikam (the descendant of David), the father is Neariah (1 Chron 3:23). For the Benjaminite in 1 Chron 9:14, it is Hassenua/Hassenua. For Asrikam in 1 Chron 8:38, the father is Azel. At least one father should be given, preferably for the primary person.; [minor] 1 Chron 9:14 mentions Asrikam as father (or ancestor) of Hashub among the Levites, not as son of Hassenua. Check the reference more carefully – in 1 Chron 9:14, Hassenua is mentioned in verse 7, while Asrikam is linked to Hashub in verse 14. The description should be corrected.; [minor] The order of keyEvents should be arranged chronologically: first Saul's descendants (1 Chron 8:38), then the war under Ahaz (2 Chron 28:7), then David's lineage through Zerubbabel (1 Chron 3:23), and finally the settlement after the exile (1 Chron 9:14, Neh 11:15).

versions.summary: Asrikam is a name borne by several individuals in the Old Testament. The most well-known was the palace administrator under King Ahaz of Judah, who was killed by the Ephraimite Zikri during the Syro-Ephraimitic War (around 735 BC). Another Asrikam is mentioned in the genealogy in 1 Chronicles as a son of Neariah and a descendant of King David through the line of Zerubbabel—an important genealogical link in the post-exilic period. In addition, an Asrikam is noted as a son of Azel among the descendants of Saul in the tribe of Benjamin, and another Asrikam is mentioned in connection with the Levites who served in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile.

versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Biblical figures named Asrikam' is somewhat generic and impersonal. A more descriptive title that highlights the diversity of individuals and their roles would have been better.; [major] The family object only indicates relationships for one of the Asrikam figures (the son of Nearjah in David's lineage), but the profile covers multiple persons. Since this is a composite profile, the family field should clarify that it refers to the Davidic Asrikam, or alternatively include father relationships for the others. For Asrikam as the son of Azel (the Benjamite), the father is 'Azel', not 'Nearjah'. The field is misleading as it stands.; [major] According to 1 Chron 3:23, Nearjah's son Asrikam had brothers Eljoenai and Hizkia, but the Hebrew text gives three sons in total. This appears correct for the Davidic line. However, the problem is that this is mixed with a profile covering multiple persons.; [minor] The role 'Levite ancestor' or 'Levite' is missing, since one of the Asrikam figures is mentioned in a Levitical context (1 Chron 9:14; Neh 11:15). The list of roles should be complete.; [minor] The era is set to 'divided-kingdom', but the persons span from the time of the divided kingdom (the palace governor under Ahaz) through the post-exilic period (David's descendant through Zerubbabel, Levite after the exile). 'Divided-kingdom' fits best for the most prominent person, but it could have been noted that the profile spans multiple eras.; [minor] The last footnote about the double entry in 1 Chron 8:38 and 9:44 is categorized as 'linguistic', but the content deals more with literary structure and editorial practice in Chronicles – 'theological' or 'other' would have been more appropriate.; [minor] The description uses the term 'official' in the title but 'palace governor' in the text. For consistency, the title should reflect the biblical title 'palace governor'.

versions.summary: Asrikam is a name belonging to at least four different persons in the Old Testament. The most prominent was the palace official (nagid habbayit) under King Ahaz of Judah, who was killed by the Ephraimite Zichri during the Syro-Ephraimitic War around 735 BC, along with the king's son Maaseiah and the royal administrator Elkanah. In the genealogical list in 1 Chronicles another Asrikam is mentioned as a son of Neariah, a descendant of King David through the line of Zerubbabel—a genealogical connection significant for messianic expectations in the post-exilic period. A third Asrikam is noted as a son of Azel among the descendants of Saul in the tribe of Benjamin. Finally, an Asrikam is mentioned in a Levitical context as an ancestor of Hashub, one of the Levites who served in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile.
versions.title: Asrikam – a name borne by several individuals in the Old Testament
versions.reason: [major] The Family field represents only one of the four individuals bearing the name Asrikam (the Davidic descendant, son of Neariah). Since the profile covers multiple persons, it is misleading to list family relations for just one of them. For a composite profile, either the most prominent individual should be represented, or this should be clearly stated. The palace official under Ahaz may be the most historically prominent, but he has no known family connections. The Neariah line is reasonable to retain, but the siblings list lacks the third brother. In 1 Chr 3:23, Neariah had three sons: Eljoenai, Hezekiah, and Asrikam – this matches, but it should be noted that this applies only to one of the individuals.; [minor] The siblings list with Eljoenai and Hezekiah is correct for Asrikam son of Neariah according to 1 Chr 3:23. This is acceptable, but it could have been clearer that this refers solely to the Davidic Asrikam.; [minor] Era is set to 'divided-kingdom', yet the profile covers multiple persons spanning from the divided kingdom (the palace official under Ahaz, c. 735 BC) to the post-exilic period (a Levitical ancestor and a Davidic descendant through Zerubbabel). While 'divided-kingdom' is acceptable for the most prominent historical figure, it is somewhat inaccurate for a profile spanning multiple eras.; [minor] The title is functional but could be more descriptive and engaging. It could be improved to highlight the most notable individual.; [minor] The summary is good and informative. It mentions 'the Syro-Ephraimite War' and all four individuals. One small improvement: the sentence about messianic expectations is theologically interesting but should be phrased carefully, as this is a genealogical note rather than an explicit messianic text.; [minor] A linguistic footnote on the meaning of the name Asrikam is missing. The Hebrew name עַזְרִיקָם (ʿAzriqam) means 'my help has risen', composed of ʿezer (help) and qam (rise). This is an interesting detail that should be included.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew name עַזְרִיקָם (ʿAzriqam) is composed of ʿezer ('help') and qam ('rise up'), and likely means 'my help has risen' or 'my kinsman has risen'. Theophoric and thanksgiving-related personal names of this type were very common in ancient Israel and express parents' gratitude for divine assistance.

Asrikam as a Levitical ancestor in 1 Chron 9:14 and Neh 11:15 places him in the context of rebuilding temple service after the Babylonian exile. The presence of the Levites in Jerusalem was crucial for restoring proper worship in the rebuilt temple.

The Hebrew expression 'nagid habbayit' (palace administrator) used for Asrikam in 2 Chron 28:7 denotes a high-ranking administrative position at the royal court. Archaeological finds of seals and bullae from the Iron Age in Judah confirm the existence of such administrative titles, attesting to a well-developed bureaucracy in the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

The Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 735–732 BC) was an alliance between Aram-Damascus and the northern kingdom of Israel against Judah, aiming to force King Ahaz into a coalition against Assyria. The war is described in 2 Kings 16, 2 Chronicles 28, and Isaiah 7. The killings of Asrikam, Maaseiah, and Elkana illustrate the severe consequences of the war for the Judean court.
